name: Emeka Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate technical documents, French into English, as a freelancer. Most days it's manuals for industrial pumps and valves: installation steps, safety warnings, torque tables. About half comes from two agencies and half straight from Halvard Pumps, a manufacturer I've worked with for three years. A few times a year they fly me to a factory to interpret during safety audits, which I enjoy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting something exactly right, where an engineer can follow my sentence with a spanner in his hand and nothing leaks. I like the factory trips, wearing the hard hat, hearing the machines. What tires me is the agencies, who cut their rate by ten percent this spring and still want it faster. My fiancée Ruth is a nurse and we're saving for a deposit on a house, so every cut stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, sensible people knew it was a tool and not a miracle. At church and with friends I'd say the work goes on as it always has. I wouldn't make a big speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safer than I do now, but not completely. The agencies would still squeeze rates, because they've learned they can. Halvard Pumps is the client that really matters, and they'd stay with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and try to move more work from the agencies to Halvard Pumps, maybe offering them a monthly retainer. I'd keep putting 400 a month into the house deposit. And I'd ask Halvard about the two factory audits next year, because those pay well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A small worry about the agencies at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the agencies cut their rate. How much does that matter to the house plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cut cost me roughly 150 a month. That's a few months later on the deposit, which Ruth and I hoped to have by the end of 2027. It's annoying, not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the AI tools at all right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I'll ask one for a first pass on a long parts list, then check every line. I don't trust AI with a safety warning, because a wrong word there can cost a man his hand.

At **church** and with friends, I'd say the work goes on as always.
think: I'd feel safer, but agencies would keep **squeezing rates** because they can.
**Halvard Pumps** is the client that matters, and they'd stay with me.
do: Offer Halvard Pumps a **monthly retainer** to replace agency work.
Keep saving **400 a month** for the house deposit.
Ask Halvard for both **factory audits** next year.
feel: He feels **steady**, with a small **agency worry** at the back.

fieldNote: His real pressure is the **house deposit**, delayed by an agency rate cut.
He uses AI **cautiously**, only for low-risk lists, never safety text.
His security rests on **one direct client**, Halvard Pumps.

steps.text: Offer Halvard Pumps a monthly retainer for manuals
Keep saving 400 a month towards the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every trade has had to change, and translators are no different. At work I'd tell Halvard I can check their machine output faster than anyone, because I know their pumps. I'd keep it polite and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the agency work goes, which is half my income. Halvard would probably buy an AI system and keep one person to check it. I'd want to be that person, but I'm not sure they'd need me full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw other translators making it work, I'd learn the system Halvard uses properly, maybe with a short course. I'd offer Halvard a fixed contract as their technical language checker. And I'd look at their field service side, because the engineers who fit pumps are always short-staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, I'll admit. I don't like not knowing where half my income goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make Halvard Pumps keep you rather than a machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the product. I've been on the Halvard Pumps factory floor and I know which valve sticks; if it's about cost only, I'm out. If they trust a person who knows that, I stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ruth change the house plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, but later and smaller. Ruth's job is safe, nurses aren't going anywhere, so we'd plan the mortgage on her pay and treat mine as extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think about families before companies. I'd say it at church, where a lot of people work in offices and would be scared too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my translating is finished within a year of it arriving. Halvard won't pay me to check what a machine does better. The only part of me with any future is the part that can stand on a factory floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask Halvard straight out about a trainee field service engineer job, fitting and repairing pumps. I'd push the deposit savings into a general emergency pot instead. And I'd sign up for a mechanical fitting certificate at the technical college, evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'm not a man who panics, but I'd be praying more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your translating is thinking work, but the factory trips are partly hands-on. How does the three-year gap play out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have three years until robots can fit pumps, around 2031, enough to train and earn as a field engineer for a while. After that, I don't know, but at least the gap gives me ground to stand on for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies racing to sell it before anyone is ready. And governments that let them. I wouldn't blame the engineers who build it; they're doing a job like me.

fieldNote: He expects to lose his **translation income** entirely and fast.

steps.text: Ask Halvard for a trainee field service engineer job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them wisely and not just complain. I'd tell younger people at church to pick up a skill they can do with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending for my translation work, just later. I'd be 32 when AGI arrives and 35 when the robots come. That's time to become a properly qualified field engineer, not just a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep translating for Halvard and start the mechanical fitting certificate part-time. By year two I'd ask to shadow their field team on a few jobs. I'd keep saving for the house, but a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a road in front of me. That's better than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What can you do that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can finish a proper qualification while still earning from translation. In two years I'd be learning in a panic; in five I can do it properly and keep the money coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told me you wait for others to prove things. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, maybe a year to see which way things go. But I wouldn't wait the whole five, that would be foolish. The fitting course starts in September either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and nobody can say they weren't told. At work I'd say let's keep the standards high while we still do it ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels manageable. I'd get a good run of translating, buy the house and maybe start a family. Then switch in my thirties with time to do it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on translating and buy the house with Ruth as planned in 2027. I'd do the fitting course in a few years, not now. And I'd keep asking Halvard about the factory trips, because that's how I'd get my foot in the field team door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, like a long winter you know is coming. Mostly I feel there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still bother with the fitting course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not yet. Maybe from 2029, when I can see how things are going. Steady wins, in my experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children, if you have them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father fixed cars and read Victor Hugo, and I'd tell my children to learn a trade as well as their books. That mix served him well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time to learn a trade properly. What would help is apprenticeships for grown men and women, paid ones, and companies like Halvard being encouraged to train their own people instead of letting them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. Translation is a craft, like carpentry. A good translation of a safety manual is a craft, and nobody gives you a medal when nothing goes wrong.

headlineQuote: A good translation of a safety manual is a craft, and nobody gives you a medal when nothing goes wrong.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** freelance French–English technical translator for pump and valve manuals.
His key client is **Halvard Pumps**, and factory audit trips are his favourite work.
He is **traditional and steady**, a churchgoer who acts once others prove things work.
He and fiancée **Ruth**, a nurse, are saving for a house deposit.
He moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** at two years, planning a hands-on field engineer switch.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, too short to learn a trade properly.
whatWouldHelp: Companies encouraged to **train their own** people rather than let them go.
